title: Automating Intune and Entra with Graph
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Apply the Graph SDK to real endpoint operations: query and act on Intune devices, manage Entra users and groups, and drive bulk changes safely with WhatIf.
objectives: Query Intune managed devices and trigger device actions through Graph
Manage Entra ID users and group memberships programmatically
Resolve a device or user object to its Graph id before acting on it
Drive dynamic vs assigned group membership and understand the difference
Add ShouldProcess so bulk scripts support -WhatIf and -Confirm
Throttle-proof a bulk operation with batching and Retry-After handling

quiz.q: Before you can POST a device action like sync or wipe, what do you usually need first?
options: The device's Graph object id, obtained by querying managedDevices
quiz.why: Graph actions target a resource by its id in the URL (for example /managedDevices/{id}/syncDevice), so you resolve the device to its id before calling the action.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between an Entra dynamic group and an assigned group?
options: There is no difference, only the name
Dynamic group membership is evaluated automatically from a rule; assigned membership is set manually
quiz.why: Dynamic groups recalculate membership from a membership rule (e.g. device OS), while assigned groups require you to add and remove members explicitly via Graph or the portal.

quiz.q: Which cmdlet triggers an Intune device sync action from the SDK?
quiz.why: Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId <id> issues the syncDevice action; many Intune actions also have an equivalent Invoke-MgGraphRequest POST.

quiz.q: Why add SupportsShouldProcess and call ShouldProcess in a bulk-change function?
options: It makes the script run faster
It is required to connect to Graph
It gives the function free -WhatIf and -Confirm so callers can preview destructive changes
quiz.why: SupportsShouldProcess plus an if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess(...)) guard lets users dry-run with -WhatIf and gate risky bulk actions with -Confirm before anything changes.

quiz.q: When Graph returns HTTP 429, what header tells you how long to wait before retrying?
quiz.answer: The Retry-After header; honour it by sleeping for that many seconds before retrying, ideally with exponential backoff.
quiz.why: 429 Too Many Requests means you are throttled; respecting Retry-After (and backing off) is the correct, supported way to keep bulk jobs running without making throttling worse.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why resolve a user to their object id rather than acting by userPrincipalName everywhere?
quiz.answer: The object id is the stable, unique key Graph uses for relationship calls like group membership, and it does not change if the userPrincipalName is renamed.
quiz.why: UPNs can be renamed and are not always accepted on relationship endpoints, so resolving to the immutable id first makes bulk scripts reliable.

body_markdown:
## Acting on Intune devices, not just reading them

Reading inventory is half the job. The other half is **taking action** — sync, restart, retire, or wipe a device. Graph actions target a resource by its **id** in the URL, so the workflow is always: resolve to id, then act.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.PrivilegedOperations.All','DeviceManagementManagedDevices.ReadWrite.All'

# Resolve the device to its Graph id
$device = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All `
    -Filter "deviceName eq 'LAP-0427'"

# Trigger a sync action against that id
Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $device.Id
```

Privileged actions like wipe require a stronger scope (`PrivilegedOperations.All`). Request it only in scripts that genuinely need it.

## Managing Entra users and groups

The same SDK manages **Entra ID**. Users, groups, and the relationships between them are all Graph resources.

```powershell
# Resolve a user to their stable object id
$user = Get-MgUser -Filter "userPrincipalName eq 'jdoe@contoso.com'"

# Add that user to a group by id
New-MgGroupMember -GroupId $groupId -DirectoryObjectId $user.Id
```

Always act on the **object id**, not the `userPrincipalName`. UPNs get renamed; the id never changes and relationship endpoints expect it.

## Dynamic vs assigned groups

An **assigned group** is one you add and remove members from by hand (or by script). A **dynamic group** recalculates its membership from a **membership rule** — for example, all Windows devices. You manage assigned groups with `New-MgGroupMember`; you manage dynamic ones by editing the rule.

```powershell
# A dynamic device group: rule, not manual members
$params = @{
    DisplayName     = 'All Windows Devices'
    MailEnabled     = $false
    MailNickname    = 'allWinDevices'
    SecurityEnabled = $true
    GroupTypes      = @('DynamicMembership')
    MembershipRule  = '(device.deviceOSType -eq "Windows")'
    MembershipRuleProcessingState = 'On'
}
New-MgGroup @params
```

## Make bulk changes safe with ShouldProcess

A script that loops over hundreds of devices must support a **dry run**. Adding `SupportsShouldProcess` to `[CmdletBinding()]` gives your function free `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm`.

```powershell
function Invoke-DeviceSyncBulk {
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess, ConfirmImpact = 'High')]
    param([Parameter(Mandatory)][object[]]$Devices)
    process {
        foreach ($d in $Devices) {
            if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($d.DeviceName, 'Sync device')) {
                Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $d.Id
            }
        }
    }
}
# Preview first, then commit:
Invoke-DeviceSyncBulk -Devices $stale -WhatIf
```

## Surviving throttling at scale

Graph throttles aggressive callers with **HTTP 429**. The response carries a **`Retry-After`** header telling you how long to pause. Honour it, ideally with backoff.

```powershell
foreach ($d in $devices) {
    try {
        Sync-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -ManagedDeviceId $d.Id -ErrorAction Stop
    }
    catch {
        if ($_.Exception.Response.StatusCode -eq 429) {
            $wait = [int]($_.Exception.Response.Headers.RetryAfter.Delta.TotalSeconds)
            Start-Sleep -Seconds ($wait ? $wait : 10)
        }
        else { throw }
    }
}
```

## Your task

Write a function `Set-StaleDeviceGroup` that finds all managed devices whose `lastSyncDateTime` is older than 30 days, resolves each to its id, and adds them to a specified assigned Entra group. Support `-WhatIf` via `SupportsShouldProcess`, request only the scopes you need, and wrap the group-add call in a try/catch that honours `Retry-After` on a 429. Run it once with `-WhatIf` to prove the preview works before any change is made.

In this lesson you stop just reading inventory and start taking action: syncing and acting on Intune devices, managing Entra users and groups, and doing it in bulk without breaking things. The two safety habits here, WhatIf and throttle handling, are what separate a hobby script from production automation.

slides.title: Splatting keeps calls readable
bullets: Build a hashtable of parameters.
Pass it with the @ splat operator.
Cleaner than long backtick-continued lines.
Easy to build parameters conditionally.
slides.narration: A quick but vital technique you just saw: splatting. Instead of a long line of parameters continued with backticks, you build a hashtable where each key is a parameter name, then pass it with the at sign splat operator. It is cleaner, and it lets you build up parameters conditionally before the call. You will use splatting constantly once you start writing real functions, so get comfortable with it now.

slides.title: Safe bulk changes with ShouldProcess
bullets: Bulk scripts must support a dry run.
SupportsShouldProcess gives free -WhatIf.
Guard each change with PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess.
ConfirmImpact High prompts on risky actions.
slides.narration: When a script loops over hundreds of devices, it must support a dry run. Add Supports Should Process to your CmdletBinding and your function gets dash WhatIf and dash Confirm for free. Then guard every change with an if P S Cmdlet dot Should Process check. Now a user can run with dash WhatIf to preview exactly what would happen and change nothing. Set Confirm Impact to High on genuinely destructive actions so it prompts before doing them. Preview first, commit second.

slides.title: Throttling and 429
bullets: Graph throttles with HTTP 429.
The Retry-After header says how long to wait.
Honour it, ideally with exponential backoff.
Never just hammer the API in a tight loop.
slides.narration: At scale, Graph will throttle you. It returns H T T P four twenty nine, too many requests, and it includes a Retry dash After header telling you how many seconds to pause. The correct, supported behaviour is to honour that header, sleep, and then retry, ideally with exponential backoff. Never just hammer the A P I in a tight loop, because that makes the throttling worse and can get your app flagged. Catch the four twenty nine, read Retry After, sleep, retry.

slides.title: Batching large jobs
bullets: Group work into chunks rather than one huge burst.
Add small pauses between batches.
Combine with Retry-After handling.
Log progress so a long run is observable.
slides.narration: Alongside honouring Retry After, proactively batch large jobs. Instead of firing thousands of requests in one burst, group the work into chunks, act on a chunk, pause briefly, then move on. Combine batching with the four twenty nine handling from the last slide and your bulk jobs become reliable. And log progress as you go, because a job that runs for twenty minutes needs to be observable so you know it is alive and where it is.
